claim: The method can monitor dry mass and dry mass density of suspension grown mammalian cells every ~75 s with 1.3% and 0.3% measurement precision, respectively.
source: To better understand mitotic cell growth and compositional changes, we develop a single-cell approach for monitoring dry mass and the density of that dry mass every ~75 s with 1.3% and 0.3% measurement precision, respectively.
evidence: Measurement precision is quantified through repeated measurements of non-growing cells and beads, as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Suspension grown mammalian cells lose dry mass following mitotic entry.
source: We find that suspension grown mammalian cells lose dry mass and increase dry mass density following mitotic entry.
evidence: Dry mass loss in early mitosis is demonstrated through single-cell measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: Suspension grown mammalian cells increase dry mass density following mitotic entry.
source: We find that suspension grown mammalian cells lose dry mass and increase dry mass density following mitotic entry.
evidence: Dry mass density increase in early mitosis is demonstrated through single-cell measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: The changes in dry mass and dry mass density display large, non-genetic cell-to-cell variability.
source: These changes display large, non-genetic cell-to-cell variability, and the changes are reversed at metaphase-anaphase transition, after which dry mass continues accumulating.
evidence: Cell-to-cell variability is shown in Figure 3C and discussed in the context of mother-daughter pairs in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The changes in dry mass and dry mass density are reversed at metaphase-anaphase transition.
source: These changes display large, non-genetic cell-to-cell variability, and the changes are reversed at metaphase-anaphase transition, after which dry mass continues accumulating.
evidence: Recovery of dry mass and dry mass density at metaphase-anaphase transition is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Dry mass continues accumulating after metaphase-anaphase transition.
source: These changes display large, non-genetic cell-to-cell variability, and the changes are reversed at metaphase-anaphase transition, after which dry mass continues accumulating.
evidence: Continued dry mass accumulation after metaphase-anaphase transition is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The change in dry mass density causes buoyant and dry mass to differ specifically in early mitosis.
source: The change in dry mass density causes buoyant and dry mass to differ specifically in early mitosis, thus reconciling existing literature on mitotic cell growth.
evidence: The difference between buoyant and dry mass in early mitosis is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and explained by Equation 1.

claim: Cells in early mitosis increase lysosomal exocytosis.
source: Mechanistically, cells in early mitosis increase lysosomal exocytosis, and inhibition of lysosomal exocytosis decreases the dry mass loss and dry mass density increase in mitosis.
evidence: Increased lysosomal exocytosis in early mitosis is demonstrated through LAMP-1 surface labeling in Figure 5.

claim: Inhibition of lysosomal exocytosis decreases the dry mass loss in mitosis.
source: Mechanistically, cells in early mitosis increase lysosomal exocytosis, and inhibition of lysosomal exocytosis decreases the dry mass loss and dry mass density increase in mitosis.
evidence: The effect of lysosomal exocytosis inhibition on dry mass loss is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Inhibition of lysosomal exocytosis decreases the dry mass density increase in mitosis.
source: Mechanistically, cells in early mitosis increase lysosomal exocytosis, and inhibition of lysosomal exocytosis decreases the dry mass loss and dry mass density increase in mitosis.
evidence: The effect of lysosomal exocytosis inhibition on dry mass density increase is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mitosis is coupled to extensive exocytosis-mediated secretion of cellular contents.
source: Overall, our work provides a new approach for monitoring single-cell dry mass and dry mass density, and reveals that mitosis is coupled to extensive exocytosis-mediated secretion of cellular contents.
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the dry mass loss data in Figure 3 and the lysosomal exocytosis data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: High concentration of D2O prevents cell proliferation and can result in cell death.
source: However, high concentration of D2O prevents cell proliferation and can result in cell death (Kampmeyer et al., 2020; Schroeter et al., 1992; Takeda et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cells can be exposed to D2O only periodically (every 75 s) and for very short durations (10–15 s) to non-invasively monitor dry mass and dry mass density over many generations without compromising cell growth and viability.
source: Here, we show that we can expose the cell to D2O only periodically (every 75 s) and for very short durations (10–15 s), thus allowing us to non-invasively monitor the dry mass and dry mass density of the same cell over many generations without compromising cell growth and viability.
evidence: This is demonstrated through multi-generational cell tracking shown in Figure 2A and cell cycle duration analysis in Figure 2B.

claim: The measured dry mass density is independent of the cell's water content.
source: By definition, the measured dry mass density is independently of the cell's water content and therefore sensitive toward changes in the relative molecular composition (dry composition), not the overall concentration of dry mass.
evidence: This is explained by the measurement principle and the definition of dry mass density (dry mass/dry volume).

claim: A decrease in the amount of cellular lipids increases the dry mass density of a cell.
source: For example, a decrease in the amount of cellular lipids increases the dry mass density of a cell, as lipids are lower in dry mass density than other cellular components.
evidence: This is based on the known physical properties of lipids having lower density than other cellular components.

claim: Buoyant mass accumulation rate is high from prophase to metaphase-anaphase transition in mammalian cells.
source: We found that buoyant mass accumulation rate is high from prophase to metaphase-anaphase transition, that is, early mitosis.
evidence: This refers to previous work by the authors (Miettinen et al., 2019).

claim: Studies using QPM have suggested that dry mass does not accumulate in early mitosis.
source: In contrast, studies using QPM have suggested that dry mass does not accumulate in early mitosis (Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015), or that cells may even experience a decrease in dry mass in early mitosis (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on citations to previous QPM studies.

claim: Cells may experience a decrease in dry mass in early mitosis according to QPM studies.
source: In contrast, studies using QPM have suggested that dry mass does not accumulate in early mitosis (Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015), or that cells may even experience a decrease in dry mass in early mitosis (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is based on citations to previous QPM studies.

claim: The approach assumes that all water within the cell is exchangeable between H2O and D2O.
source: Importantly, our approach assumes that all water within the cell is exchangeable between H2O and D2O.
evidence: This is a stated assumption of the measurement method.

claim: The dry volume measurement is distinct from the excluded cell volume detected by measuring cell volume following strong hyperosmotic shocks.
source: Accordingly, our dry volume measurement is distinct from the excluded cell volume detected by measuring cell volume following strong hyperosmotic shocks, which does not remove all water from the intracellular space.
evidence: This is explained as a distinction between measurement approaches based on the completeness of water removal.

claim: Cells constantly exchange their water content, causing intracellular H2O to be exchanged to D2O.
source: Cells constantly exchange their water content, causing intracellular H2O to be exchanged to D2O.
evidence: This is a known biological property of cells and is fundamental to the measurement principle.

claim: The densities of the extracellular fluid are not constant due to fluid mixing between measurements.
source: The densities of the extracellular fluid are not constant due to fluid mixing between measurements, but this is accounted for by directly measuring the extracellular solution density, that is, the baseline frequency of the SMR, together with every buoyant mass measurement.
evidence: This describes a technical aspect of the measurement approach and how it is addressed.

claim: The dry mass measurement error is ~1.3%.
source: We therefore estimate our dry mass measurement error to be ~1.3%, which is comparable to current state-of-the-art QPM measurements (Liu et al., 2020; Reed et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on measurements of non-growing cells and beads shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dry mass measurement error is comparable to current state-of-the-art QPM measurements.
source: We therefore estimate our dry mass measurement error to be ~1.3%, which is comparable to current state-of-the-art QPM measurements (Liu et al., 2020; Reed et al., 2011).
evidence: This comparison is made with reference to previous QPM studies.

claim: The dry mass density measurement error is ~0.3%.
source: For dry mass density measurements, we estimate our measurement error to be ~0.3%.
evidence: This is based on measurements of non-growing cells and beads shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are no other single-cell methods capable of quantifying dry mass density.
source: We are not aware of any other single-cell methods capable of quantifying this metric.
evidence: This is stated as the authors' assessment of the current state of the field.

claim: Direct experimental evidence suggests that cells normally exchange their water content within ~1 s.
source: Direct experimental evidence suggests that cells normally exchange their water content within ~1 s (Potma et al., 2001; Quirk et al., 2003; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous experimental studies.

claim: Cells are capable of exchanging all of their water volume within 0.1–2.5 s based on aquaporin water permeability calculations.
source: This suggested that cells are capable of exchanging all of their water volume within 0.1–2.5 s, depending on the reported aquaporin water permeability.
evidence: This is based on calculations using reported aquaporin properties from Gravelle et al., 2013; Hashido et al., 2007; Yang and Verkman, 1997; Denker et al., 1988.

claim: In typical measurements, a cell is exposed to D2O for 10–15 s, which should enable complete water exchange.
source: In our typical measurement, a cell is exposed to D2O for 10–15 s, which should enable complete water exchange.
evidence: This is based on the comparison with the calculated water exchange times and is validated in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The measured dry mass and dry mass density were independent of the time in D2O-based media.
source: Whether examining end-point measurements of single L1210 cells in a population (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), a single-cell trace of a live L1210 cell cooled to +4°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) or a single-cell trace of an L1210 cell at +37°C (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C), the measured dry mass and dry mass density were independent of the time in D2O-based media.
evidence: This is demonstrated through experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The rate of intracellular water exchange is not limiting the measurements.
source: Thus, the rate of intracellular water exchange is not limiting our measurements, as also suggested by previous results in bacteria and yeast (Feijó Delgado et al., 2013).
evidence: This conclusion is based on the data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and previous work in bacteria and yeast.

claim: L1210, BaF3, and S-Hela cells can tolerate continuous exposure to up to 30% D2O without changes to proliferation rate under normal culture conditions.
source: Under normal culture conditions, all three cell lines can tolerate continuous exposure to up to 30% D2O without changes to proliferation rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through cell proliferation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells were still able to proliferate at higher D2O concentrations, albeit slowly.
source: Cells were still able to proliferate at higher D2O concentrations, albeit slowly.
evidence: This is observed in the proliferation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cell cycle durations of wild-type L1210 cells remained comparable to previous observations in the SMR in the absence of D2O.
source: Under these conditions, cell cycle durations of wild-type (wt) L1210 cells remained comparable to what we have observed previously in the SMR in the absence of D2O (Miettinen et al., 2019; Mu et al., 2020; Figure 2B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through cell cycle duration measurements shown in Figure 2B and compared to previous studies.

claim: FUCCI L1210 cells showed slightly increased cell cycle durations when periodically exposed to D2O.
source: However, when examining FUCCI (hGeminin-mKO) cell cycle reporter expressing L1210 cells, we observed slightly increased cell cycle durations.
evidence: This is shown in the cell cycle duration data in Figure 2B.

claim: The duration of mitosis and cytokinesis was systematically shorter when cells were periodically exposed to D2O than in previous SMR experiments.
source: In addition, we observed that the duration of mitosis and cytokinesis was systematically shorter when cells were periodically exposed to D2O than what we have previously observed in other SMR experiments (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Exponential fits are a better model for dry mass growth in interphase than linear fits for L1210 cells.
source: We compared linear and exponential growth models using Akaike information criterion (AIC) and found that exponential fits are a better model for our data in 37 out of 39 interphases (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through AIC analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Instantaneous dry mass growth rates increased as a function of dry mass in L1210 cells, consistent with exponential growth.
source: Consistent with exponential growth, instantaneous dry mass growth rates (pg/hr) increased as a function of dry mass (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through growth rate analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There were no systematic changes in cell's dry mass at division in ancestral L1210 lineages with ≥3 full cell cycles.
source: We then examined the stability of cell size homeostasis in ancestral L1210 lineages with ≥3 full cell cycles. We did not observe systematic changes in cell's dry mass at division (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through lineage tracking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Limited D2O exposure may influence cell proliferation rate but does not radically alter cell size and growth regulation.
source: Together, these results show that we can monitor the dry mass and dry mass density of single cells over long time periods using our heavy water-based measurement approach, and while limited D2O exposure may influence cell proliferation rate, it does not radically alter cell size and growth regulation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the cell cycle and growth data shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is a high degree of correlation (R2 >0.97) between dry mass and buoyant mass for L1210, BaF3, and S-Hela cell populations.
source: We observed a high degree of correlation (R2 >0.97) for L1210, BaF3, and S-Hela cell populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through population-level measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: There is a very high degree of correlation (R2~0.99) between dry mass and buoyant mass in interphase of L1210 cells.
source: We then correlated dry mass and buoyant mass within our L1210 single-cell growth traces and observed a very high degree of correlation in interphase of each cell (R2~0.99), but lower and more variable correlations in mitosis and cytokinesis (R2~0.5–0.9) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B&C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through single-cell tracking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B&C.

claim: There are lower and more variable correlations (R2~0.5–0.9) between dry mass and buoyant mass in mitosis and cytokinesis of L1210 cells.
source: We then correlated dry mass and buoyant mass within our L1210 single-cell growth traces and observed a very high degree of correlation in interphase of each cell (R2~0.99), but lower and more variable correlations in mitosis and cytokinesis (R2~0.5–0.9) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B&C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through single-cell tracking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B&C.

claim: Buoyant mass is an accurate proxy for cell's dry mass in interphase, but not necessarily in mitosis.
source: Together, these observations indicate that buoyant mass is an accurate proxy for cell's dry mass in interphase, but not necessarily in mitosis.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Dry mass density displays little variability within proliferating cell populations, with coefficient of variability around 1.6% for L1210, BaF3, and S-Hela cells.
source: Indeed, in our population level data, dry mass density displayed little variability, with coefficient of variability around 1.6% for L1210, BaF3, and S-Hela cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through population-level measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The variability in dry mass density is approximately 15-fold less than the variability observed for dry mass.
source: This is approximately 15-fold less variability than observed for dry mass.
evidence: This is calculated from the data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The low variability in dry mass density within a proliferating cell population represents the tight regulation of cells' molecular composition.
source: The low variability in dry mass density within a proliferating cell population represents the tight regulation of cells' molecular composition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the low variability observed in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Many, but not all, L1210 cells lost dry mass and dry volume following mitotic entry.
source: Curiously, we observed that many, but not all, L1210 cells lost dry mass and, especially, dry volume following mitotic entry, resulting in increased dry mass density in early mitosis (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through single-cell measurements shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: The loss of dry mass and dry volume resulted in increased dry mass density in early mitosis.
source: Curiously, we observed that many, but not all, L1210 cells lost dry mass and, especially, dry volume following mitotic entry, resulting in increased dry mass density in early mitosis (Figure 3A–C; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through single-cell measurements shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: The mitotic dry mass and dry mass density changes were observed in both wt and FUCCI L1210 cells.
source: This was observed in both wt and FUCCI L1210 cells, although the FUCCI cells displayed larger changes in mitosis (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of wt and FUCCI cells in Figure 3B.

claim: FUCCI L1210 cells displayed larger changes in mitosis than wt L1210 cells.
source: This was observed in both wt and FUCCI L1210 cells, although the FUCCI cells displayed larger changes in mitosis (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparison of wt and FUCCI cells in Figure 3B.

claim: On average, FUCCI L1210 cells lost ~4% of dry mass in early mitosis.
source: On average, the FUCCI L1210 cells lost ~4% of dry mass and increased dry mass density by ~2.5%, and these changes took place in approximately 15 min (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is quantified from the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: On average, FUCCI L1210 cells increased dry mass density by ~2.5% in early mitosis.
source: On average, the FUCCI L1210 cells lost ~4% of dry mass and increased dry mass density by ~2.5%, and these changes took place in approximately 15 min (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is quantified from the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The dry mass and dry mass density changes in early mitosis took place in approximately 15 min.
source: On average, the FUCCI L1210 cells lost ~4% of dry mass and increased dry mass density by ~2.5%, and these changes took place in approximately 15 min (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is quantified from the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the most extreme cases, cells lost ~8% of their dry mass while increasing dry mass density by ~4%.
source: In the most extreme cases, cells lost ~8% of their dry mass while increasing dry mass density by ~4%.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cells recovered their lost dry mass at metaphase-anaphase transition.
source: These changes were transient, as cells recovered their lost dry mass and decreased their dry mass density at metaphase-anaphase transition (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the population average data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Cells decreased their dry mass density at metaphase-anaphase transition.
source: These changes were transient, as cells recovered their lost dry mass and decreased their dry mass density at metaphase-anaphase transition (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the population average data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The recovery of dry mass at metaphase-anaphase transition was faster than the dry mass growth observed prior to mitosis.
source: The recovery of dry mass at metaphase-anaphase transition was faster than the dry mass growth observed prior to mitosis, suggesting that this 'recovery growth' is distinct from normal cell growth.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The 'recovery growth' at metaphase-anaphase transition is distinct from normal cell growth.
source: The recovery of dry mass at metaphase-anaphase transition was faster than the dry mass growth observed prior to mitosis, suggesting that this 'recovery growth' is distinct from normal cell growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the faster rate of dry mass recovery compared to normal growth shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Over 10% of the total dry mass accumulated in the cell cycle takes place in mitosis and cytokinesis for L1210 cells.
source: The total amount of dry mass accumulated in mitosis and cytokinesis was large, over 10% of the dry mass accumulated in the whole cell cycle (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is quantified from the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The extent of mitotic dry mass loss in early mitosis was coupled to the extent of corresponding dry mass density increase.
source: The extent of mitotic dry mass loss in early mitosis was coupled to the extent of corresponding dry mass density increase (Figure 3E).
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated in Figure 3E.

claim: The increase in dry mass density uncoupled buoyant mass and dry mass measurements in early mitosis.
source: Importantly, the increase in dry mass density uncoupled buoyant mass and dry mass measurements (Equation 1), causing buoyant mass to increase in early mitosis even in the cells which lost dry mass (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through example traces in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C and explained by Equation 1.

claim: Buoyant mass increased in early mitosis even in cells which lost dry mass.
source: Importantly, the increase in dry mass density uncoupled buoyant mass and dry mass measurements (Equation 1), causing buoyant mass to increase in early mitosis even in the cells which lost dry mass (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through example traces in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: Approximately 7% of all L1210 cells measured (10 out of 67 cells) displayed little to no dry mass density increase in early mitosis.
source: Approximately 7% of all L1210 cells measured (10 out of 67 cells) displayed little to no dry mass density increase in early mitosis.
evidence: This is calculated from the data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mother-daughter pairs were observed where the mother cell displayed mitotic changes in dry mass and dry mass density but the daughter cell did not, or vice versa.
source: We also observed mother-daughter pairs where the mother cell displayed mitotic changes in its dry mass and dry mass density but the daughter cell did not, or vice versa (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through example traces in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: The difference in mitotic behavior between individual cells did not correlate with experiment-specific noise levels.
source: The difference in mitotic behavior between individual cells did not correlate with experiment-specific noise levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through correlation analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The mitotic dry mass and dry mass density changes are not required for a successful cell division.
source: Furthermore, since the dry mass and dry mass density changes were not present in all cells, they are not required for a successful cell division.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some cells divide without these changes.

claim: On average, BaF3 cells did not lose dry mass in mitosis but growth rather stopped during early mitosis.
source: While some individual BaF3 cells lost ~4% of their dry mass during early mitosis, on average the BaF3 cells did not lose dry mass in mitosis but growth rather stopped during early mitosis, which was followed by a rapid recovery at metaphase-anaphase transition (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through BaF3 cell measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-E.

claim: Some individual BaF3 cells lost ~4% of their dry mass during early mitosis.
source: While some individual BaF3 cells lost ~4% of their dry mass during early mitosis, on average the BaF3 cells did not lose dry mass in mitosis but growth rather stopped during early mitosis, which was followed by a rapid recovery at metaphase-anaphase transition (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-E).
evidence: This is observed in the individual cell data for BaF3 cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-E.

claim: BaF3 cells displayed a rapid recovery of dry mass at metaphase-anaphase transition.
source: While some individual BaF3 cells lost ~4% of their dry mass during early mitosis, on average the BaF3 cells did not lose dry mass in mitosis but growth rather stopped during early mitosis, which was followed by a rapid recovery at metaphase-anaphase transition (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through BaF3 cell measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-E.

claim: On average, THP-1 cells lost ~5% of their dry mass in early mitosis.
source: In THP-1 cells, on average, cells lost ~5% of their dry mass, which was also recovered at metaphase-anaphase transition (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F-J).
evidence: This is quantified from THP-1 cell measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3F-J.

claim: THP-1 cells recovered their lost dry mass at metaphase-anaphase transition.
source: In THP-1 cells, on average, cells lost ~5% of their dry mass, which was also recovered at metaphase-anaphase transition (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F-J).
evidence: This is demonstrated through THP-1 cell measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3F-J.

claim: In both BaF3 and THP-1 cells, dry mass density transiently increased in early mitosis.
source: In both cell types, dry mass density transiently increased in early mitosis.
evidence: This is demonstrated through measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The mitotic loss of dry mass and increase in dry mass density are not specific to L1210 cells.
source: Thus, the mitotic loss of dry mass and increase in dry mass density are not specific to L1210 cells.
evidence: This is concluded from observations in BaF3 and THP-1 cells shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Early mitosis is coupled to previously unrecognized secretion of cellular components.
source: More broadly, our dry mass measurements suggest that early mitosis is coupled to previously unrecognized secretion of cellular components.
evidence: This is inferred from the dry mass loss observed in early mitosis shown in Figure 3.

claim: STLC-treated cells displayed slightly larger, but statistically not significantly different, loss of dry mass upon mitotic entry compared to control cells.
source: When monitoring STLC-treated cells, we observed slightly larger, but statistically not significantly different, loss of dry mass and increase in dry mass density upon mitotic entry as in control cells (Figure 4B&C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through STLC treatment experiments shown in Figure 4B&C.

claim: STLC-treated cells displayed slightly larger, but statistically not significantly different, increase in dry mass density upon mitotic entry compared to control cells.
source: When monitoring STLC-treated cells, we observed slightly larger, but statistically not significantly different, loss of dry mass and increase in dry mass density upon mitotic entry as in control cells (Figure 4B&C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through STLC treatment experiments shown in Figure 4B&C.

claim: Mitotically arrested cells did not recover their dry mass or dry mass density.
source: However, the mitotically arrested cells did not recover their dry mass or dry mass density, and following the initial changes the STLC-treated cells displayed slow dry mass accumulation and steady dry mass density for the rest of the mitotic arrest.
evidence: This is demonstrated through STLC treatment experiments shown in Figure 4B&C.

claim: STLC-treated cells displayed slow dry mass accumulation and steady dry mass density following the initial changes.
source: However, the mitotically arrested cells did not recover their dry mass or dry mass density, and following the initial changes the STLC-treated cells displayed slow dry mass accumulation and steady dry mass density for the rest of the mitotic arrest.
evidence: This is demonstrated through STLC treatment experiments shown in Figure 4B&C.

claim: The increase in dry mass density and decrease in dry mass take place before the completion of prometaphase.
source: These results verify that the increase in dry mass density and decrease in dry mass take place before the completion of prometaphase, and that mitotic progression is required for the rapid recovery of dry mass and dry mass density.
evidence: This is concluded from the STLC arrest experiments shown in Figure 4B&C, where cells are arrested in prometaphase.

claim: Mitotic progression is required for the rapid recovery of dry mass and dry mass density.
source: These results verify that the increase in dry mass density and decrease in dry mass take place before the completion of prometaphase, and that mitotic progression is required for the rapid recovery of dry mass and dry mass density.
evidence: This is concluded from the STLC arrest experiments shown in Figure 4B&C.

claim: Barasertib-treated cells displayed slightly lower, but statistically not significantly different, loss of dry mass compared to untreated FUCCI L1210 cells.
source: The Barasertib-treated cells displayed slightly lower, but statistically not significantly different, loss of dry mass and increase in dry mass density as untreated FUCCI L1210 cells (Figure 4E&F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Barasertib treatment experiments shown in Figure 4E&F.

claim: Barasertib-treated cells displayed slightly lower, but statistically not significantly different, increase in dry mass density compared to untreated FUCCI L1210 cells.
source: The Barasertib-treated cells displayed slightly lower, but statistically not significantly different, loss of dry mass and increase in dry mass density as untreated FUCCI L1210 cells (Figure 4E&F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Barasertib treatment experiments shown in Figure 4E&F.

claim: The duration of mitosis was lengthened in some Barasertib-treated cells, resulting in slower recovery of dry mass and dry mass density.
source: The duration of mitosis was lengthened in some Barasertib-treated cells, resulting in slower recovery of dry mass and dry mass density.
evidence: This is observed in the Barasertib treatment experiments shown in Figure 4E&F.

claim: The mitotic changes in cell's dry mass and dry mass density cannot be fully explained by cell elongation and furrowing.
source: Thus, the mitotic changes in cell's dry mass and dry mass density cannot be fully explained by cell elongation and furrowing, although cell elongation and furrowing (or Aurora B activity) could still have an influence on dry mass and dry mass density dynamics in mitosis.
evidence: This is concluded from the Barasertib treatment experiments shown in Figure 4E&F.

claim: Cell elongation and furrowing (or Aurora B activity) could still have an influence on dry mass and dry mass density dynamics in mitosis.
source: Thus, the mitotic changes in cell's dry mass and dry mass density cannot be fully explained by cell elongation and furrowing, although cell elongation and furrowing (or Aurora B activity) could still have an influence on dry mass and dry mass density dynamics in mitosis.
evidence: This is suggested as a possibility based on the Barasertib treatment experiments.

claim: Mitotic cells swell from prophase to metaphase and recover in anaphase.
source: Another major morphological change that mitotic cells undergo is the mitotic cell swelling, where cells take up water and can increase their total volume by 10–20% (Son et al., 2015; Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015). This takes place simultaneously with the dry mass changes, that is, cells swell from prophase to metaphase and recover in anaphase.
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Son et al., 2015; Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015).

claim: Mitotic cells can increase their total volume by 10–20% during mitotic cell swelling.
source: Another major morphological change that mitotic cells undergo is the mitotic cell swelling, where cells take up water and can increase their total volume by 10–20% (Son et al., 2015; Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Son et al., 2015; Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015).

claim: FUCCI L1210 cells swell significantly in early mitosis.
source: This revealed that the FUCCI L1210 cells swell significantly in early mitosis, but this is near completely prevented by EIPA treatment (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through water volume measurements shown in Figure 4G.

claim: EIPA treatment near completely prevents mitotic cell swelling in FUCCI L1210 cells.
source: This revealed that the FUCCI L1210 cells swell significantly in early mitosis, but this is near completely prevented by EIPA treatment (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is demonstrated through water volume measurements shown in Figure 4G.

claim: EIPA treatment did not change the amount of dry mass lost or dry mass density increased in early mitosis when compared to control cells.
source: However, when we monitored the dry mass and density of FUCCI L1210 cells in the presence of EIPA, we did not observe any changes in the amount of dry mass lost or dry mass density increased in early mitosis when compared to control cells (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through EIPA treatment experiments shown in Figure 4E&F.

claim: The mitotic dry mass and dry mass density changes do not require mitotic cell swelling.
source: Therefore, the mitotic dry mass and dry mass density changes do not require mitotic cell swelling.
evidence: This is concluded from the EIPA treatment experiments shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: It remains possible that mitotic dry mass/density changes and mitotic cell swelling share a common driving mechanism.
source: However, it remains possible that these two phenotypes share a common driving mechanism.
evidence: This is suggested as a possibility despite the EIPA treatment results.

claim: Macromolecules constitute most of cell's dry mass.
source: Macromolecules would be the most likely form of mass lost, as they constitute most of cell's dry mass.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge of cell composition.

claim: Inorganic ions constitute only ~1% of cell's dry mass.
source: In contrast, inorganic ions are an unlikely form of dry mass lost, as these constitute only ~1% of cell's dry mass (Cooper and Hausman, 2013).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a textbook (Cooper and Hausman, 2013).

claim: The secretion of lactate is not increased in mitotic L1210 cells.
source: Cells could secrete metabolites or small molecules in mitosis, but at least the secretion of lactate, a key metabolite secreted by cells, is not increased in mitotic L1210 cells (Kang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work (Kang et al., 2020).

claim: It seems unlikely that cells could lose large amounts of ions and/or small molecules while increasing osmotic pressure required for mitotic cell swelling.
source: Furthermore, it seems unlikely that cells could lose large amounts of ions and/or small molecules while increasing osmotic pressure, which is required for the mitotic cell swelling.
evidence: This is based on reasoning about osmotic pressure requirements.

claim: Most studies have found that endocytosis stops in mitosis from mitotic entry until anaphase.
source: Most studies have found that endocytosis stops in mitosis, more specifically from mitotic entry until anaphase (Fielding et al., 2012; Schweitzer et al., 2005; Warren et al., 1984).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Fielding et al., 2012; Schweitzer et al., 2005; Warren et al., 1984).

claim: Contradictory results on mitotic endocytosis have been reported.
source: However, contradictory results on mitotic endocytosis have also been reported (Boucrot and Kirchhausen, 2007).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a study with different findings (Boucrot and Kirchhausen, 2007).

claim: Lysosomal exocytosis has been suggested to increase in late mitosis.
source: Changes in exocytosis have not been studied in similar detail during mitosis, but lysosomal exocytosis, where cells secrete lysosomal contents by fusing lysosomes with the plasma membrane (Reddy et al., 2001), has been suggested to increase in late mitosis (Nugues et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Reddy et al., 2001; Nugues et al., 2018).

claim: Lysosomal exocytosis has been shown to secrete fatty acids out of the cell.
source: Notably, lysosomal exocytosis has also been shown to secrete fatty acids (which are low in dry mass density) out of the cell (Cui et al., 2021), which could increase the dry mass density of a cell.
evidence: This is based on a citation to a previous study (Cui et al., 2021).

claim: Fatty acids are low in dry mass density.
source: Notably, lysosomal exocytosis has also been shown to secrete fatty acids (which are low in dry mass density) out of the cell (Cui et al., 2021), which could increase the dry mass density of a cell.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of fatty acids.

claim: Secretion of fatty acids could increase the dry mass density of a cell.
source: Notably, lysosomal exocytosis has also been shown to secrete fatty acids (which are low in dry mass density) out of the cell (Cui et al., 2021), which could increase the dry mass density of a cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the low density of fatty acids.

claim: Mitotic cells had more LAMP-1 on their surface than interphase cells.
source: Quantifications of the microscopy indicated that mitotic cells had more LAMP-1 on their surface than interphase cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through microscopy quantifications shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The amount of LAMP-1 on cell surface increased from early mitosis to late mitosis.
source: Furthermore, the amount of LAMP-1 on cell surface increased from early mitosis (prophase, prometaphase, and metaphase) to late mitosis (anaphase) (Figure 5B), indicating that cell surface LAMP-1 accumulates throughout early mitosis.
evidence: This is demonstrated through microscopy quantifications shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Cell surface LAMP-1 accumulates throughout early mitosis.
source: Furthermore, the amount of LAMP-1 on cell surface increased from early mitosis (prophase, prometaphase, and metaphase) to late mitosis (anaphase) (Figure 5B), indicating that cell surface LAMP-1 accumulates throughout early mitosis.
evidence: This is concluded from the increase in LAMP-1 from early to late mitosis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The finding that cell surface LAMP-1 accumulates throughout early mitosis is in contrast to a previous report suggesting that lysosomal exocytosis increases specifically in late mitosis.
source: This is in contrast to the previous report suggesting that lysosomal exocytosis increases specifically in late mitosis (Nugues et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a contrast to the findings in Nugues et al., 2018.

claim: Cells arrested to early mitosis displayed higher levels of LAMP-1 on their surface than cells arrested to G2.
source: Cells arrested to early mitosis displayed higher levels of LAMP-1 on their surface than cells arrested to G2 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through flow cytometry measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In BaF3 cells, LAMP-1 labeling was higher in early mitosis than in G2.
source: We also examined cell surface LAMP-1 immunolabeling in BaF3 and THP-1 cells after cell cycle synchronizations to G2 or early mitosis. In both cell lines, LAMP-1 labeling was higher in early mitosis than in G2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: In THP-1 cells, LAMP-1 labeling was higher in early mitosis than in G2.
source: We also examined cell surface LAMP-1 immunolabeling in BaF3 and THP-1 cells after cell cycle synchronizations to G2 or early mitosis. In both cell lines, LAMP-1 labeling was higher in early mitosis than in G2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated through measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lysosome exocytosis is increased in early mitosis.
source: Thus, lysosome exocytosis is increased in early mitosis.
evidence: This is concluded from the LAMP-1 surface labeling data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Both brefeldin A and vacuolin-1 prevented the accumulation of LAMP-1 on plasma membrane in L1210 cells.
source: Both chemicals prevented the accumulation of LAMP-1 on plasma membrane in L1210 cells (Figure 6A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1), indicating that lysosomal exocytosis was inhibited.
evidence: This is demonstrated through LAMP-1 labeling experiments shown in Figure 6A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lysosomal exocytosis was inhibited by brefeldin A and vacuolin-1.
source: Both chemicals prevented the accumulation of LAMP-1 on plasma membrane in L1210 cells (Figure 6A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1), indicating that lysosomal exocytosis was inhibited.
evidence: This is concluded from the prevention of LAMP-1 accumulation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Both brefeldin A and vacuolin-1 decreased the mitotic changes to cells' dry mass.
source: We then monitored the dry mass and dry mass density of FUCCI L1210 cells in the presence of brefeldin A or vacuolin-1. Both chemicals decreased the mitotic changes to cells' dry mass and dry mass density (Figure 6B&C) without preventing cell divisions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through treatment experiments shown in Figure 6B&C.

claim: Both brefeldin A and vacuolin-1 decreased the mitotic changes to cells' dry mass density.
source: We then monitored the dry mass and dry mass density of FUCCI L1210 cells in the presence of brefeldin A or vacuolin-1. Both chemicals decreased the mitotic changes to cells' dry mass and dry mass density (Figure 6B&C) without preventing cell divisions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through treatment experiments shown in Figure 6B&C.

claim: Brefeldin A and vacuolin-1 did not prevent cell divisions.
source: We then monitored the dry mass and dry mass density of FUCCI L1210 cells in the presence of brefeldin A or vacuolin-1. Both chemicals decreased the mitotic changes to cells' dry mass and dry mass density (Figure 6B&C) without preventing cell divisions.
evidence: This is observed in the treatment experiments shown in Figure 6B&C.

claim: Brefeldin A and vacuolin-1 did not cause clear changes to the baseline dry mass density of cells.
source: The chemicals did not cause clear changes to the baseline dry mass density of cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lysosomal exocytosis is, at least partly, responsible for the loss of dry mass in early mitosis.
source: Thus, lysosomal exocytosis is, at least partly, responsible for the loss of dry mass and increased dry mass density in early mitosis.
evidence: This is concluded from the inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 6B&C.

claim: Lysosomal exocytosis is, at least partly, responsible for the increased dry mass density in early mitosis.
source: Thus, lysosomal exocytosis is, at least partly, responsible for the loss of dry mass and increased dry mass density in early mitosis.
evidence: This is concluded from the inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 6B&C.

claim: This is the first method capable of non-invasively measuring cell's dry volume or dry mass density.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first method capable of non-invasively measuring cell's dry volume or dry mass density.
evidence: This is stated as the authors' assessment of the novelty of their method.

claim: Dry mass density measurements lack molecular specificity.
source: While dry mass density measurements lack molecular specificity, they are non-invasive, quantitative, and have high temporal resolution.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the method.

claim: Dry mass density measurements are non-invasive, quantitative, and have high temporal resolution.
source: While dry mass density measurements lack molecular specificity, they are non-invasive, quantitative, and have high temporal resolution.
evidence: These are stated as advantages of the method.

claim: QPM has several advantages over the authors' method, including higher throughput and suitability for adherent cells.
source: QPM has several advantages over our method, including higher throughput and suitability for adherent cells, but our method is comparable in precision and has high temporal resolution.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between methods.

claim: The authors' method is comparable to QPM in precision and has high temporal resolution.
source: QPM has several advantages over our method, including higher throughput and suitability for adherent cells, but our method is comparable in precision and has high temporal resolution.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the authors' method.

claim: The authors' method is not limited by phototoxicity.
source: Our method is also not limited by phototoxicity.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the method.

claim: The mitotic dry mass dynamics differ from previously reported buoyant mass dynamics due to a transient change in dry mass density in early mitosis.
source: Importantly, the mitotic dry mass dynamics differ from our previously reported buoyant mass dynamics due to a transient change in dry mass density in early mitosis (Equation 1).
evidence: This is explained by the relationship between buoyant mass, dry mass, and dry mass density in Equation 1.

claim: This finding reconciles previous mitotic buoyant mass measurements with QPM-based dry mass measurements by others.
source: This finding reconciles our previous mitotic buoyant mass measurements (Miettinen et al., 2019) with the QPM-based dry mass measurements by others (Liu et al., 2020; Zlotek-Zlotkiewicz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a reconciliation of seemingly contradictory findings.

claim: For L1210 cells, over 10% of the total dry mass growth in the cell cycle takes place in mitosis and cytokinesis.
source: The overall dry mass growth remains high in mitosis and cytokinesis, and for L1210 cells over 10% of the total dry mass growth in the cell cycle takes place in mitosis and cytokinesis.
evidence: This is quantified from the data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Average cell growth rates in mitosis and cytokinesis are comparable to those observed in interphase.
source: This supports our previous main conclusion that average cell growth rates in mitosis and cytokinesis are comparable to those observed in interphase, which is consistent with the high protein synthesis rates reported for unperturbed mitosis (Coldwell et al., 2013; Miettinen et al., 2019; Stonyte et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as support for a previous conclusion and is consistent with cited studies on protein synthesis.

claim: High protein synthesis rates have been reported for unperturbed mitosis.
source: This supports our previous main conclusion that average cell growth rates in mitosis and cytokinesis are comparable to those observed in interphase, which is consistent with the high protein synthesis rates reported for unperturbed mitosis (Coldwell et al., 2013; Miettinen et al., 2019; Stonyte et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Coldwell et al., 2013; Miettinen et al., 2019; Stonyte et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2019).

claim: In interphase, dry mass density is conserved, making buoyant mass an excellent proxy for dry mass.
source: In interphase, dry mass density is conserved, making buoyant mass an excellent proxy for dry mass.
evidence: This is concluded from the high correlation between buoyant and dry mass in interphase shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: A loss of dry mass in mitosis has been reported in adherent mammalian cells studied using QPM.
source: Importantly, a loss of dry mass in mitosis has been reported in adherent mammalian cells studied using QPM (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022), but the higher temporal resolution of our results enables us to examine this phenotype in more detail.
evidence: This is based on citations to previous QPM studies (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022).

claim: The higher temporal resolution of the authors' results enables examination of mitotic dry mass loss in more detail than previous studies.
source: Importantly, a loss of dry mass in mitosis has been reported in adherent mammalian cells studied using QPM (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2022), but the higher temporal resolution of our results enables us to examine this phenotype in more detail.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of the current study.

claim: The measurement approach decreased the duration of mitosis and cytokinesis.
source: However, our measurement approach decreased the duration of mitosis and cytokinesis, which could potentially influence the dry mass dynamics we observe in mitosis.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The decrease in mitotic duration is contradictory to previous studies which show that mitosis is prolonged by D2O exposure.
source: This decrease in mitotic duration is contradictory to previous studies which show that mitosis is prolonged by D2O exposure (Lamprecht et al., 1990; Takahashi and Sato, 1983), possibly due to the brief but repeated D2O exposure in our measurements.
evidence: This is stated as a contradiction to previous studies (Lamprecht et al., 1990; Takahashi and Sato, 1983).

claim: The decrease in mitotic duration is possibly due to the brief but repeated D2O exposure in the measurements.
source: This decrease in mitotic duration is contradictory to previous studies which show that mitosis is prolonged by D2O exposure (Lamprecht et al., 1990; Takahashi and Sato, 1983), possibly due to the brief but repeated D2O exposure in our measurements.
evidence: This is suggested as a possible explanation for the observed difference.

claim: Cells are able to recover dry mass at a high rate at metaphase-anaphase transition.
source: Our results also show that cells are able to recover dry mass at a high rate at metaphase-anaphase transition.
evidence: This is demonstrated in the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Lysosomal exocytosis is typically followed by endocytosis, which removes lysosomal membranes from plasma membrane.
source: Interestingly, the exocytosis of lysosomes is typically followed by endocytosis, which removes lysosomal membranes from plasma membrane (Idone et al., 2008; Tam et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Idone et al., 2008; Tam et al., 2010).

claim: Compensatory endocytosis could explain the rapid recovery of dry mass at metaphase-anaphase transition.
source: Such a compensatory endocytosis could explain the rapid recovery of dry mass at metaphase-anaphase transition, but further quantitative studies on endo- and exocytosis are needed to confirm this.
evidence: This is suggested as a possible explanation based on known biology of lysosomal exocytosis.

claim: The magnitude of dry mass density increase in mitosis was large.
source: The magnitude of dry mass density increase in mitosis was large.
evidence: This is stated based on the measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: Similar magnitude changes in dry mass density have been previously observed when perturbing proliferation in mammalian cells.
source: We have previously observed similar magnitude changes in dry mass density when perturbing proliferation in mammalian cell (Feijó Delgado et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous work (Feijó Delgado et al., 2013).

claim: Cells would have to secrete ~1/3 of their lipid content in early mitosis to increase dry mass density by 2.5%, based on calculations.
source: Assuming a typical mammalian cell composition and typical macromolecule dry mass densities (Alberts, 2008; Feijó Delgado et al., 2013), we calculated the degree of lipid loss needed to increase dry mass density by 2.5%. This suggested that cells would have to secrete ~1/3 of their lipid content in early mitosis.
evidence: This is calculated based on typical cell composition and macromolecule densities from Alberts, 2008; Feijó Delgado et al., 2013.

claim: Secretion of ~1/3 of lipid content could be achieved via lysosomal exocytosis of lipids.
source: This could be achieved via lysosomal exocytosis of lipids.
evidence: This is suggested based on the calculation and known mechanisms of lipid secretion.

claim: Lipid droplets are frequently trafficked into and degraded in lysosomes.
source: Lipid droplets, the main lipid storages inside cells, are frequently trafficked into and degraded in lysosomes (Singh et al., 2009), and lipid droplets can also be secreted via lysosomal exocytosis (Minami et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Singh et al., 2009; Minami et al., 2022).

claim: Lipid droplets can be secreted via lysosomal exocytosis.
source: Lipid droplets, the main lipid storages inside cells, are frequently trafficked into and degraded in lysosomes (Singh et al., 2009), and lipid droplets can also be secreted via lysosomal exocytosis (Minami et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on a citation to a previous study (Minami et al., 2022).

claim: It seems likely that the mitotic dry mass density increase also involves secretion of other low dry mass density components and/or a minor, transient increase in high dry mass density components in early mitosis.
source: However, it seems likely that the mitotic dry mass density increase also involves secretion of other low dry mass density components (e.g. lipoproteins, specific metabolites) and/or a minor, transient increase in high dry mass density components (e.g. RNAs, specific proteins) in early mitosis.
evidence: This is suggested as a likely scenario based on the magnitude of the observed changes.

claim: CDK1 activity has been suggested to drive a transient increase in protein and RNA content in early mitosis.
source: Indeed, CDK1 activity has been suggested to drive a transient increase in protein and RNA content in early mitosis (Asfaha et al., 2022; Clemm von Hohenberg et al., 2022; Miettinen et al., 2019; Shuda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Asfaha et al., 2022; Clemm von Hohenberg et al., 2022; Miettinen et al., 2019; Shuda et al., 2015).

claim: Lysosomal exocytosis acts in plasma membrane repair.
source: (1) Lysosomal exocytosis acts in plasma membrane repair (Reddy et al., 2001), and lysosomal exocytosis could enable a temporarily increase in plasma membrane area for mitotic cell swelling.
evidence: This is based on a citation to a previous study (Reddy et al., 2001).

claim: Lysosomal exocytosis could enable a temporary increase in plasma membrane area for mitotic cell swelling.
source: (1) Lysosomal exocytosis acts in plasma membrane repair (Reddy et al., 2001), and lysosomal exocytosis could enable a temporarily increase in plasma membrane area for mitotic cell swelling.
evidence: This is hypothesized based on the known role of lysosomal exocytosis in membrane repair.

claim: Lysosomal exocytosis is used for secretion of various proteins and enzymes into the extracellular space.
source: (2) Lysosomal exocytosis is used for secretion of various proteins and enzymes into the extracellular space (Blott and Griffiths, 2002), and mitotic cells may secrete extracellular matrix modifying enzymes in order to ensure an appropriate physical milieu for cell division.
evidence: This is based on a citation to a previous study (Blott and Griffiths, 2002).

claim: Mitotic cells may secrete extracellular matrix modifying enzymes to ensure an appropriate physical milieu for cell division.
source: (2) Lysosomal exocytosis is used for secretion of various proteins and enzymes into the extracellular space (Blott and Griffiths, 2002), and mitotic cells may secrete extracellular matrix modifying enzymes in order to ensure an appropriate physical milieu for cell division.
evidence: This is hypothesized as a possible function of mitotic lysosomal exocytosis.

claim: Lysosomal exocytosis has been shown to clear the cell of excessive/toxic cellular proteins and lipids, including α-synuclein and tau.
source: (3) Lysosomal exocytosis has been shown to clear the cell of excessive/toxic cellular proteins and lipids, including α-synuclein (Tsunemi et al., 2019) and tau (Xu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Tsunemi et al., 2019; Xu et al., 2021).

claim: Mitotic lysosomal exocytosis may act as a 'reset' that enables daughter cells to be born with a minimal load of useless/harmful contents.
source: Mitotic lysosomal exocytosis may act as a 'reset' that enables the daughter cells to be born with a minimal load of useless/harmful contents.
evidence: This is hypothesized as a possible function of mitotic lysosomal exocytosis.

claim: Non-dividing cells, such as neurons, could be more prone to suffer from excessive/toxic protein and lipid buildup.
source: Consequently, non-dividing cells, such as neurons, could be more prone to suffer from excessive/toxic protein and lipid buildup, and the mechanism(s) that promote(s) mitotic lysosomal exocytosis could act as candidate drug target(s) for promoting cellular clearance of toxic/excess components.
evidence: This is hypothesized based on the proposed 'reset' function of mitotic lysosomal exocytosis.

claim: The mechanism(s) that promote(s) mitotic lysosomal exocytosis could act as candidate drug target(s) for promoting cellular clearance of toxic/excess components.
source: Consequently, non-dividing cells, such as neurons, could be more prone to suffer from excessive/toxic protein and lipid buildup, and the mechanism(s) that promote(s) mitotic lysosomal exocytosis could act as candidate drug target(s) for promoting cellular clearance of toxic/excess components.
evidence: This is suggested as a potential therapeutic application.

claim: Lysosomal exocytosis is perturbed in a variety of lysosomal and lipid storage disorders.
source: Lysosomal exocytosis is also perturbed in a variety of lysosomal and lipid storage disorders (reviewed in Samie and Xu, 2014; Settembre and Ballabio, 2014), and lysosomal exocytosis can drive the cellular expulsion of chemotherapeutics out of cancer cells (Vyas et al., 2022; Zhitomirsky and Assaraf, 2017).
evidence: This is based on citations to review articles (Samie and Xu, 2014; Settembre and Ballabio, 2014).

claim: Lysosomal exocytosis can drive the cellular expulsion of chemotherapeutics out of cancer cells.
source: Lysosomal exocytosis is also perturbed in a variety of lysosomal and lipid storage disorders (reviewed in Samie and Xu, 2014; Settembre and Ballabio, 2014), and lysosomal exocytosis can drive the cellular expulsion of chemotherapeutics out of cancer cells (Vyas et al., 2022; Zhitomirsky and Assaraf, 2017).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies (Vyas et al., 2022; Zhitomirsky and Assaraf, 2017).

claim: Understanding the mechanism(s) of mitotic lysosomal exocytosis could have implications for lysosomal and lipid storage disorders as well as cancer chemotherapy resistance.
source: Understanding the mechanism(s) of mitotic lysosomal exocytosis could have implications for these diseases as well.
evidence: This is suggested based on the known roles of lysosomal exocytosis in these diseases.
